passage: Come, kanna, sit. When I was ten, a new girl joined our school in Madurai. Her name was Sarika, and she walked with two wooden crutches. At break, all of us ran to play kho-kho and she sat alone on the step, turning her bangles. Nobody was mean. We just forgot her. After three days I felt so bad I couldn't eat my lemon rice. So I went and asked, 'I'm Lavanya. Will you be our timekeeper? You have a watch.' She shouted the times louder than our teacher! Later we made up a sitting game with pebbles so she could win too. Sarika and I wrote letters to each other for forty years. That is what making room means, kanna.

qa.q: What job did young Lavanya offer Sarika at break?
qa.a: Lavanya asked Sarika to be the timekeeper for kho-kho because Sarika had a watch.

qa.q: Why couldn't young Lavanya eat the lemon rice?
qa.a: Lavanya felt guilty that everyone had forgotten Sarika, who sat alone on the step for three days.

qa.q: Which of young Lavanya's ideas worked, and why?
qa.a: They gave her a real role in the game and then invented a pebble game where she could play and win too.

qa.q: How might Sarika have felt on those first three days at break?
qa.a: She probably felt lonely and left out, sitting by herself while everyone ran off to play.

grounding: An elder recalls making room for a new classmate who used crutches.

passage: Rain hammered the tin roof, so PE moved into the crowded school hall. Forty children shouted at once. Vikas noticed Deepak, the new boy with the hearing aids, standing by the wall looking lost. Sir had explained the relay rules, but in this noise Deepak had clearly caught nothing. Vikas walked over and stood right in front of him so Deepak could see his face. 'Relay. Run, touch the wall, come back, tap the next hand,' he said slowly, and showed it with his arms. Deepak nodded and grinned. 'Our team?' 'Our team,' said Vikas. When Deepak got tapped, he ran like wind. Afterwards he said, 'Thanks. Nobody faces me.'

qa.q: Where was PE held that day, and why?
qa.a: It was held in the crowded school hall because rain was hammering the roof.

qa.q: What does Deepak's comment 'Nobody faces me' suggest about how he felt before?
qa.a: It suggests he often felt shut out because people spoke without letting him see their faces, so he missed things.

qa.q: What small step made the difference for Deepak?
qa.a: Vikas stood face to face, spoke slowly and showed the rules with gestures before inviting him onto his team.

qa.q: What would have changed if Vikas hadn't walked over?
qa.a: Deepak would likely have stayed by the wall, confused about the rules and left out of the relay.

grounding: Shows a child including a new classmate with a hearing difference despite a noisy setting.

passage: It was woodwork class in a school outside Gothenburg, and the room smelled of pine shavings. Hana, eleven, was sawing a board for her birdhouse. Two boys at the next bench snickered. 'Careful, she'll cut her nails.' Anders, who shared her bench, didn't laugh. He had been about to grab her saw to help, then stopped. 'Want me to hold the board steady, or are you fine?' Hana blew hair out of her eyes. 'Fine. But you can pass the sandpaper.' He passed it. When the boys snickered again, Anders said, 'Her cut is straighter than yours, Olle.' Olle looked at his wobbly board and went quiet. Hana smiled at the sawdust.

qa.q: What was Hana making in woodwork class?
qa.a: She was sawing a board for her birdhouse.

qa.q: Why do you think Anders stopped before grabbing Hana's saw?
qa.a: He seemed to realise she might not want help and that taking over could look like he thought she couldn't do it.

qa.q: What did Anders do that showed respect?
qa.a: He asked before helping, accepted her 'fine', and calmly answered the teasing with a fact instead of mockery.

qa.q: How might Hana have felt if Anders had laughed along with the boys?
qa.a: She would likely have felt more alone and embarrassed, and less willing to use the tools in front of them.

grounding: Shows courtesy and respect for boundaries between classmates of different genders, without stereotyped roles.

passage: The Saturday embroidery club at the community centre had eleven girls and, from this week, one boy. Anirban, twelve, sat at the end of the long table with a hoop and red thread. Two girls whispered and giggled. 'Did he come for the biscuits?' Dolma, who was helping Mrs Bose hand out needles, heard. She sat down beside him. 'Your chain stitch is neater than mine. Show me?' He showed her, ears pink. Later he reached for her scissors, then stopped. 'Can I borrow these?' 'Sure.' When the giggling started again, Dolma said, 'He's here to stitch, same as us.' The whisperers went back to their flowers.

qa.q: How many girls were in the embroidery club?
qa.a: There were eleven girls.

qa.q: What do Anirban's pink ears suggest he was feeling?
qa.a: He was probably embarrassed by the giggling but also pleased that Dolma asked him to show his stitch.

qa.q: What did Dolma do that a helper could copy?
qa.a: She sat with the new member, praised his real skill, and calmly said he belonged there instead of mocking back.

qa.q: How might the two whispering girls see Anirban after Dolma spoke?
qa.a: They might start seeing him as just another club member rather than someone to laugh at.

grounding: Shows respectful interaction across genders without mockery, including asking before borrowing.

passage: Asif bhai's stationery shop in the lane behind the Dadar market was packed with parents buying school supplies. Irawati, ten, paid for a geometry box with a hundred-rupee note. He was answering three customers at once and handed her change without looking. On the steps outside, she counted. Too much. He'd given her change for a five hundred. Her heart jumped. Nobody had seen. She could buy the glitter pens. She took four steps toward home. Then she thought of Asif bhai counting his cash box tonight, frowning. She squeezed back through the crowd. 'Bhaiya, you gave me extra.' He stared, then laughed. 'Arre, in this rush! Thank you, beti.'

qa.q: What did Irawati buy at the shop?
qa.a: She bought a geometry box.

qa.q: What made Irawati turn back after four steps?
qa.a: She imagined Asif bhai frowning over his cash box that night and felt it would be wrong to keep money no one knew about.

qa.q: What does Irawati's choice show about acting well when no one is watching?
qa.a: It shows she let her own sense of right, not the fear of being caught, decide what she did.

qa.q: How might Asif bhai see Irawati the next time she visits his shop?
qa.a: He would probably remember her as an honest child and trust her warmly.

grounding: Shows a child returning extra change though she could never have been caught.

passage: 'Mama?' Joseph hovered in the kitchen doorway. Anjali looked up from the dosa pan. 'You're quiet. What happened?' 'When I was cycling in the compound, my pedal scraped Mr D'Costa's scooter. There's a long line now.' 'Did he see?' 'Nobody saw. Nobody was there.' 'So why are you telling me?' Joseph twisted his T-shirt. 'Because it's his scooter. And I keep thinking about it.' Anjali turned off the flame. 'That thinking is your good sense. What do you want to do?' 'Tell him? He'll shout.' 'Maybe. Want me to come?' 'Stand near. But I'll say it.' 'Deal.' They walked down together. Joseph's voice shook, but he said every word.

qa.q: What did Joseph's pedal scrape?
qa.a: It scraped Mr D'Costa's scooter and left a long line.

qa.q: Why did Joseph tell his mother even though nobody saw?
qa.a: He felt uneasy and kept thinking about the damage to someone else's scooter, so he wanted to put it right.

qa.q: How did Anjali support Joseph without taking over?
qa.a: She stayed calm, asked what he wanted to do and offered to stand near while letting him speak for himself.

qa.q: If you were Mr D'Costa, what would you want?
qa.a: You would probably want the truth, and you might be less angry because the boy came himself to admit it.

grounding: Shows a child admitting a mistake no one saw, supported by a parent.

passage: The school bus left in ten minutes, and class six was still sitting in silence. Someone had drawn a moustache on the principal's photo, and nobody owned up, so Mrs Rao had cancelled sports day practice for all of them. Siddharth, eleven, raised his hand. 'Ma'am, can I say something quickly?' She nodded. 'The drawing was wrong. But forty kids losing practice for one person's joke feels too big. And some of us weren't even in the room.' Pradeep whispered, 'You'll get us in more trouble.' Mrs Rao tapped her pen. 'What would be fair, then?' 'Only those who were here stay back and clean it. Everyone else practises.' She thought, then agreed.

qa.q: Why had Mrs Rao cancelled sports day practice?
qa.a: Someone drew a moustache on the principal's photo and nobody owned up.

qa.q: What was Pradeep worried about when Siddharth spoke up?
qa.a: Pradeep feared that questioning the teacher would make things worse for the whole class.

qa.q: What made Siddharth's argument persuasive?
qa.a: He admitted the drawing was wrong, explained why the punishment was too big, and offered a fairer alternative.

qa.q: How might the children who weren't in the room see the new decision?
qa.a: They would likely feel relieved and that they had been treated fairly at last.

grounding: Shows a child debating whether a group punishment is proportionate and fair to all, under time pressure.

passage: In their Jaipur colony, the cricket rule was clear: hit the ball into Mrs Kulkarni's garden and you were banned for a week. On Sunday, Anand, nine, swung hard and the ball sailed over her hedge. He knew the rule, but his stomach dropped. 'A whole week? It was an accident!' Disha, his twelve-year-old sister, was captain. 'Rules are rules.' 'But when Bunty hit it there on purpose last month, he also got one week. That's the same for doing it on purpose and by mistake.' Disha frowned. Other kids gathered. 'Okay,' she said slowly, 'so maybe first accident is just out. On purpose, one week.' Everyone voted. Anand fetched the ball and said sorry to Mrs Kulkarni.

qa.q: What was the colony rule about Mrs Kulkarni's garden?
qa.a: Anyone who hit the ball into her garden was banned for a week.

qa.q: How did Anand feel when the ball went over the hedge?
qa.a: He felt a sinking dread, since he knew the rule, and then it seemed unfair because it was an accident.

qa.q: What made Anand's point about Bunty a strong one?
qa.a: He showed the same punishment was given for an accident and a deliberate act, which isn't proportionate.

qa.q: Why might Disha have changed her mind as captain?
qa.a: She saw that treating an accident like a deliberate hit wasn't fair to everyone, and a vote kept the group together.

grounding: Shows children debating whether a punishment is proportionate and revising a rule fairly.

passage: Tuesday: In health class, Shalini Ma'am talked about bodies changing, and some boys giggled at the word 'periods'. Remi, as Lalremsiami's friends called her, stared at her desk with burning cheeks and asked nothing. Next Friday: In the last period, Remi felt something damp and saw a spot on her skirt in the washroom. She froze. Then she remembered Ma'am saying, 'Come to me, any time.' She went to the counsellor's room, whispering. Shalini Ma'am calmly gave her a pad, a spare skirt and a paper bag. 'This is your body growing, exactly as it should. Nothing to be ashamed of.' The Monday after: Remi packed a small pouch in her bag and showed her friend Esther where she kept it.

qa.q: What did Shalini Ma'am give Remi in the counsellor's room?
qa.a: She gave her a pad, a spare skirt and a paper bag.

qa.q: What does Remi's burning face in health class suggest she was feeling?
qa.a: She seemed embarrassed and a bit ashamed, especially with the boys giggling, so she asked nothing.

qa.q: How could a school make moments like Remi's Friday easier for children?
qa.a: It could make sure every child knows a calm, trusted adult to go to and keep spare supplies ready without fuss.

qa.q: How might Esther feel when Remi shows her the pouch?
qa.a: Esther might feel trusted and more ready for any changes of their own, seeing that it can be talked about without shame. 🤍

grounding: Shows a girl moving from shame to understanding a body change calmly, with privacy and practical hygiene.

passage: Seema, you asked why I always say 'ask me anything'. Let me tell you. When I was twelve, in our village, nobody explained anything to girls. One morning I saw blood and thought I was dying. I hid in the cowshed and cried. My mother just said, 'Keep quiet, don't tell anyone,' and gave me old cloth. I felt dirty for months, as if I'd done something wrong. Only when my aunt came visiting did she sit me down, say 'Leela, listen,' and tell me it was my body growing up, that it happens to every girl. I promised myself my girls would know before. So, Seema, your voice-changing brother, your own body, all of it: ask me anything.

qa.q: Where did young Leela hide when she first saw the blood?
qa.a: She hid in the cowshed and cried.

qa.q: Why did young Leela feel dirty for months?
qa.a: Nobody explained what was happening and she was told to keep quiet, so she believed she had done something wrong.

qa.q: What is Leela doing differently for Seema?
qa.a: She is inviting open questions about body changes early, so Seema can learn facts before any fear or shame sets in.

qa.q: How might Seema feel hearing Leela's story?
qa.a: Seema might feel sad for young Leela and more comfortable bringing questions to Leela.

grounding: An elder recalls puberty without information and now offers a young listener shame-free understanding.

passage: Coach's note, junior badminton, Saturday. Pallavi (10) reached the final of the club tournament today. For six weeks she has come early to practise her low serve against the wall, even on days her friends skipped. Today it showed: her serves were clean. She lost the final in three games to a taller girl from Andheri. At the last point she threw her head back and I saw her blinking hard. But she walked straight to the net, shook hands and said, 'Good game, your smashes were amazing.' Only after that did she sit on the bench and cry into her towel. I sat beside her and said nothing for a while. On Monday we'll look at her backhand. — Coach Himani

qa.q: What did Pallavi practise early for six weeks?
qa.a: She practised her low serve against the wall.

qa.q: What does Pallavi's blinking and later crying suggest she felt?
qa.a: She was deeply disappointed about losing but held back her tears until she had congratulated her opponent.

qa.q: Why was Coach Himani's choice to sit silently a good one?
qa.a: It let Pallavi feel her disappointment with support nearby, without rushing her or turning it into a lesson.

qa.q: How might the girl from Andheri remember the final?
qa.a: She would likely remember Pallavi as a kind, fair opponent who praised her smashes even after losing.

grounding: A coach records a child building skill through repeated practice and losing gracefully.

passage: Wednesday. Chess club tournament today. I have practised knight moves every night for a month, even the boring puzzles Uncle printed for me. I won my first two games! Then I played Afreen. She is ten, one year younger than me, and I thought it would be easy. She trapped my queen in fifteen moves. I felt like knocking all the pieces off the board. My face was so hot. But I remembered what Sir says, 'Shake hands first, feel later.' So I said 'good game' through my teeth. It came out weird. Afreen said 'good game' back and showed me where I went wrong. Actually useful. Still annoyed. Practising queen safety tomorrow. — Zubin

qa.q: How many moves did it take Afreen to trap Zubin's queen?
qa.a: Afreen trapped Zubin's queen in fifteen moves.

qa.q: How can you tell Zubin was angry after losing to Afreen?
qa.a: Zubin's face was hot, Zubin felt like knocking the pieces off the board and said 'good game' through gritted teeth.

qa.q: What did Zubin do right after the loss, even though it was hard?
qa.a: Zubin followed Sir's rule, shook hands and listened to Afreen's tips, then planned to practise what went wrong.

qa.q: How might Afreen see Zubin's 'good game'?
qa.a: She may have noticed it sounded strained but still felt respected, since Zubin listened when she pointed out the mistake. 🙂

grounding: A child writes about practising a skill and managing to lose gracefully despite anger.

passage: Farhan's cricket match in the Lucknow colony ground was at four. At lunch he skipped Ammi's rajma and rice and ate two packets of chips and a fizzy drink from the corner shop. By the second over he felt heavy and yawny, and he dropped an easy catch. His friend Naveen was running between the wickets like a rocket. 'What did you eat?' Farhan panted at the drinks break. 'Roti, dal, a banana,' Naveen said. 'Same as always.' Farhan's tummy grumbled even though he'd eaten plenty. That night he ate the rajma, twice. Next Saturday, before the match, he asked Ammi for a banana too. He didn't drop anything.

qa.q: What did Farhan eat instead of the rajma and rice?
qa.a: He ate two packets of chips and a fizzy drink.

qa.q: Why did Farhan ask Naveen what he had eaten?
qa.a: He was wondering why he felt heavy and slow while Naveen had so much energy, and suspected food made a difference.

qa.q: What worked well in how Farhan changed his habits?
qa.a: He noticed his own body's signals, compared with a friend and tried a simple swap before the next match.

qa.q: How might Ammi see Farhan asking for a banana?
qa.a: She would probably be pleased and a little amused that he chose it himself without her nagging. 😊

grounding: Shows a child linking his food choices to energy for play.

passage: 'Papa, noodles again tonight?' Mohit looked up from the chopping board. 'Divyansh, we had them yesterday and the day before.' 'They're the best food in the world.' 'They're tasty, I agree. How did you feel at football today?' Divyansh made a face. 'Tired. I sat down after ten minutes.' 'Hmm. Do you know what your body uses for running?' 'Food?' 'Fuel. Noodles alone are like filling a car with half the petrol. Dal, vegetables, curd, eggs, those help you grow and run.' 'Can noodles have vegetables in them?' Mohit laughed. 'Now you're thinking. Sunday special: noodles with peas and carrots. Tonight, khichdi.' Divyansh groaned. 'Okay. But extra ghee.'

qa.q: How long did Divyansh last at football before sitting down?
qa.a: Divyansh sat down after ten minutes because he felt tired.

qa.q: What does Divyansh's question about vegetables in noodles suggest he was thinking?
qa.a: Divyansh was starting to look for a way to keep a favourite food while getting more of the fuel a growing body needs.

qa.q: What did Papa do well to help Divyansh think about food?
qa.a: He agreed noodles are tasty and linked food to how Divyansh felt at football, instead of banning them.

qa.q: What would change if Papa had simply said 'No noodles ever'?
qa.a: Divyansh might have felt punished and craved noodles more, without learning why other foods help.

grounding: Shows a parent helping a child connect food choices to energy and growth.

passage: The storm had knocked out the power, Ammi was stuck at work across the flooded road, and Ganga, eleven, was in charge. Then her little brother Farhan tripped on the dark stairs and cut his knee on the step. He wailed. Blood ran down to his sock. Ganga's hands shook, but she remembered the school first-aid class. She used her phone torch, washed the cut with clean water from the bottle, pressed a clean cloth on it and held it, firmly. 'Hold still, brave boy.' The bleeding slowed. She found the list on the fridge: Ammi, Nani, the neighbour, and the emergency number at the top. She called Ammi and described the cut clearly.

qa.q: What did Ganga use to see in the dark?
qa.a: She used her phone torch.

qa.q: How can you tell Ganga was scared even while she helped?
qa.a: Her hands were shaking, but she kept going because she remembered what she had learned.

qa.q: Which of Ganga's steps could other children learn from?
qa.a: She cleaned the cut, pressed a clean cloth on it, kept her brother calm and then used the contact list to call an adult.

qa.q: If the cut had been much worse, what might Ganga have done differently?
qa.a: She would call the emergency number at the top of the list or the neighbour for help straight away, as well as Ammi.

grounding: Shows a child handling a small injury during a power cut and knowing whom to call.

passage: Sarika, nine, was coming up the stairs of her Kolkata building with a bag of bread when she heard a thin cry. Irawati aunty, who lived on the second floor, was sitting on the landing, holding her ankle. 'I slipped, baby. I can't get up.' Sarika wanted to pull her up, but remembered her teacher's words: don't move someone who's hurt, get help. She ran down, banged on the guard's cabin and shouted for her father on the phone. 'Papa, Irawati aunty fell, she can't stand. Second-floor landing, Block C.' Papa said he was calling for help and coming. Sarika went back up, sat beside aunty and held her cold hand until the grown-ups came.

qa.q: Where had Irawati aunty fallen?
qa.a: She fell on the second-floor landing of the building.

qa.q: Why did Sarika not pull Irawati aunty up, even though she wanted to?
qa.a: She remembered her teacher saying not to move someone who's hurt, and chose to get help instead.

qa.q: What made Sarika's phone call to Papa useful?
qa.a: She said clearly what happened and exactly where, so help could be sent to the right place.

qa.q: What was it like for Irawati aunty to have Sarika sit beside her?
qa.a: It likely comforted her and made her less frightened while she waited alone in pain. 🙏

grounding: Shows a child responding to an emergency by getting help and giving a clear location.

passage: Counsellor's note, class four, after the body-safety session. At break Ramesh (9) waited until the room emptied. He said an older cousin had been asking him to play a 'secret game' and touched him where his swimsuit covers. Ramesh told him no and went away. He told his mother, but she said, 'Don't make up stories about family.' He said, 'You told us to keep telling until someone believes.' I told him I believed him, that it was not his fault and that he did right to keep telling. I did not ask for details. I informed the principal the same day and followed our school's safeguarding steps, including a call with his father. I will check on Ramesh tomorrow. — Jatin Sir

qa.q: What did Ramesh's mother say when he first told her?
qa.a: She said, 'Don't make up stories about family.'

qa.q: What does Ramesh waiting until the room was empty suggest about how he felt?
qa.a: He was probably scared and embarrassed and needed privacy, but he was determined to be heard.

qa.q: What did Jatin Sir do that was right?
qa.a: He believed Ramesh, told him it wasn't his fault, did not push for details and followed the school's safety steps the same day.

qa.q: How might it feel for Ramesh to hear 'I believe you' after not being believed at home?
qa.a: It would likely bring huge relief and help him trust that telling was worth it. 🤍

grounding: Shows a child who said no to unsafe touch and kept telling trusted adults until he was believed.

passage: Thursday. Today in school we learned the swimsuit rule: nobody can touch the parts a swimsuit covers, and nobody can ask you to keep secrets about touching. Ma'am said good secrets are like surprise parties; bad secrets make your tummy feel wrong. We traced our hands and wrote one trusted adult on each finger. Mine: Mummy, Papa, Baljeet mama, Class Ma'am, and Dadi. Ma'am said if one person doesn't listen, tell the next finger, and the next. I thought about the time Chachi kept squeezing my cheeks and I hated it. Mummy said I'm allowed to say 'no thank you'. I stuck the hand picture on my cupboard. — Lokesh

qa.q: How many trusted adults did Lokesh write on the traced hand?
qa.a: Five: Mummy, Papa, Baljeet mama, Class Ma'am and Dadi.

qa.q: What might Lokesh have been feeling when he remembered Chachi squeezing Lokesh's cheeks?
qa.a: Lokesh remembered hating it and was likely relieved to know it is okay to say no to touch that feels unwanted.

qa.q: Why is the 'tell the next finger' idea helpful for children?
qa.a: It shows that if one adult doesn't listen, they should keep telling others until someone helps.

qa.q: How might Lokesh's parents feel seeing the hand picture on the cupboard?
qa.a: They might feel glad Lokesh knows the rules and that they are among the trusted adults on the list.

grounding: A child records learning body-boundary rules and naming trusted adults to tell.

passage: Sahil kept his pocket money in an old steel tiffin box under his bed in their Chennai flat. The goal was written on a sticky note on the lid: 'Cricket bat, ₹900.' After four months he had ₹640. On Saturday, at the Pondy Bazaar pavement stalls with his sister Dolma, he saw a yo-yo that lit up blue and green. ₹150. 'Ooh,' he breathed. 'Need or want?' Dolma asked, grinning. 'Want. Really, really want.' He turned it over in his hand. It would be fun for a day or two. The bat would be for the whole season. He put it back. On the way home, he did buy new chappals, because his old ones had snapped. That was a need.

qa.q: How much money had Sahil saved after four months?
qa.a: He had saved ₹640.

qa.q: What was Sahil thinking as he turned the yo-yo over in his hand?
qa.a: He was weighing a day or two of fun against the bat he wanted for the whole season.

qa.q: What helped Sahil stick to his savings goal?
qa.a: Having the goal written on the lid, and pausing to ask whether the yo-yo was a need or a want.

qa.q: How might Dolma see her brother's choice?
qa.a: She might be impressed that he walked away from something he really wanted, all by himself.

grounding: Shows a child saving toward a goal and choosing between a need and an impulse want.

passage: 'Dadu, look! Two hundred rupees from Mashi for my birthday!' Jeevan dadu lowered his newspaper. 'Very rich man now. Plans?' 'Stickers! The shiny football ones. A whole pack is two hundred.' 'Hmm. And your pencil box?' Anirban looked at it. The lid hung by one hinge. 'It still works. Sort of.' 'Sort of.' Dadu smiled. 'What did you say you wanted most last month?' 'A proper football. But that's so much money.' 'What if some goes in this jar every time?' Dadu tapped an empty pickle jar. Anirban chewed his lip. 'Hundred in the jar, fifty for a pencil box, fifty for stickers?' 'Your money, your choice.' 'Deal. I'm writing FOOTBALL on the jar.'

qa.q: How much birthday money did Anirban get from Mashi?
qa.a: He got two hundred rupees.

qa.q: What does Anirban chewing his lip suggest?
qa.a: He was torn between wanting stickers now and saving for the football he wanted most, and was working out a plan.

qa.q: Why did Dadu's approach help Anirban decide?
qa.a: He asked questions and suggested a jar but left the final choice to Anirban, so the plan felt like his own.

qa.q: What would change if Dadu had taken the money away to save for him?
qa.a: Anirban might have felt cheated and wouldn't have practised deciding between needs, wants and a saving goal.

grounding: Shows a child dividing money between a need, a want and a saving goal.
